stem: A stock index stands at 4,000. The risk-free rate is 4% per year and the index dividend yield is 1.5% per year, both continuously compounded. The theoretical 6-month futures price is closest to:

rationale.A: Incorrect. 3,950.31 uses e^(−(r − q)T), discounting instead of compounding the net carry.
rationale.B: Incorrect. 4,080.81 ignores the dividend yield and grows the index at the full 4% rate.
rationale.C: Correct. The index is carried forward at the net rate r − q = 2.5% for half a year.
rationale.D: Incorrect. 4,111.53 adds the dividend yield to the risk-free rate instead of subtracting it.

stem: The spot exchange rate is 1.2500 USD per GBP. The USD risk-free rate is 3% and the GBP risk-free rate is 5%, both continuously compounded. The 1-year forward exchange rate (USD per GBP) is closest to:
explanation: F = S e^((r_USD − r_GBP)T) = 1.25 × e^(0.03 − 0.05) = 1.25 × e^(−0.02) = 1.2252. The higher-yielding pound trades at a forward discount.

rationale.A: Incorrect. 1.2753 swaps the two rates, using r_GBP − r_USD.
rationale.B: Incorrect. 1.2500 assumes the forward equals spot, ignoring the interest rate differential.
rationale.C: Incorrect. 1.1890 discounts at the GBP rate only, forgetting that the USD rate grows the price.
rationale.D: Correct. With USD per GBP, the domestic (USD) rate comes first: 1.25 × e^(−0.02) = 1.2252.

stem: A non-dividend-paying stock trades at USD 50 and the 1-year risk-free rate implies a theoretical forward price of USD 52.56. A dealer quotes a 1-year forward price of USD 51.00. Which strategy captures a riskless profit?
options: Short-sell the stock, invest the proceeds at the risk-free rate and take a long forward position
Borrow USD 50, buy the stock and take a short forward position
Buy the stock with borrowed money and take a long forward position
Short-sell the stock, invest the proceeds and take a short forward position
explanation: The quoted forward is below fair value, so buy the cheap forward and sell the asset synthetically priced higher: reverse cash-and-carry. At year end the invested proceeds grow to 52.56, the long forward costs 51.00 to buy back the share, and 1.56 is locked in.

rationale.A: Correct. Reverse cash-and-carry: buy the underpriced forward and short the stock, earning 52.56 − 51.00 = 1.56 at delivery.
rationale.B: Incorrect. Cash-and-carry is used when the forward is too expensive; here it would lose 52.56 − 51.00 = 1.56.
rationale.C: Incorrect. Being long both the stock and the forward doubles the exposure; it is not a hedge.
rationale.D: Incorrect. Short stock plus short forward is a doubled short position, not an arbitrage.

stem: An investor holds a long forward contract with a delivery price of USD 102 and 6 months to maturity. The current forward price for the same delivery date is USD 105. The risk-free rate is 4% per year with continuous compounding. The value of the investor's contract is closest to:

rationale.A: Incorrect. 3.06 compounds the gain forward instead of discounting it to today.
rationale.B: Correct. The 3-dollar gain is received at maturity, so its present value is 3 × e^(−0.02) = 2.94.
rationale.C: Incorrect. 3.00 is the undiscounted difference; the gain is not received until delivery.
rationale.D: Incorrect. 0.92 discounts only the new forward price (105e^(−0.02) − 102), mixing present and future values.
